entries.title: The Enterprise Case for Open-Weight Models on Databricks
entries.summary: As field engineers at Databricks, we spend our days inside enterprise AI deployments,...
entries.content:
A thought-piece on how Unity AI Gateway and Omnigent combine lower costs, data sovereignty, operational autonomy, and model flexibility to meet the changing demands of enterprise AI strategy.

by Jay Palaniappan, Elise Gonzales, Tanner Waggoner, Toby Messinger and Will Middlebrook

  • Open-weight models now approach frontier-class intelligence at lower cost while giving enterprises data sovereignty and operational autonomy.
  • Unity AI Gateway serves open-weight, frontier, and external models through one governed API with fast inference, smart routing, fallbacks, and budget controls.

As field engineers at Databricks, we spend our days inside enterprise AI deployments, where we’ve observed a clear shift in strategy. After two years of standardizing on single frontier model providers, companies are reevaluating their approach due to seven key pressures:

1. Spend is not generating sufficient returns. AI budgets have outpaced revenue and cost savings, prompting a need for better unit economics [1].

2. Model rankings have changed repeatedly since 2023. The best model for coding, reasoning, and extraction changes month to month, and the top intelligence ranking has changed hands 20+ times since May 2023 [2]. Architectures tied to a single provider make it harder to adopt a better model as rankings change.

3. Frontier guardrails can block legitimate work. Model guardrails imposed by AI labs can refuse legitimate tasks, such as analyzing live malware or reproducing an exploit to patch it, a limitation discovered in the recent Hugging Face incident [6][7]. When Hugging Face responders fed real attack logs and exploit payloads to hosted frontier models for analysis, the guardrails refused, and the team ran the analysis on an open-weight model (GLM 5.2) instead.

4. Data retention policies have evolved and may continue to do so. Some frontier providers have deviated from zero-data-retention (ZDR) policies, such as the 30-day minimum retention introduced with Anthropic's frontier tier [8]. For enterprises whose compliance policy was written around the principle that "no prompt or completion is ever stored," an upstream policy change could introduce problems and potentially require a system change.

5. Companies want visibility into and control over model governance. Demand is growing for end-to-end visibility and governance across AI models. Customers want searchable records of model inputs, outputs, errors, and agent actions to enable teams to evaluate accuracy and improve performance, as well as centralized controls to protect sensitive data and intellectual property.

6. The harness matters as much as the model. Databricks’ research shows that the scaffolding around a model, its harness of prompts, tools, and control flow, changes measured performance. In Databricks’ own benchmark, the same model scored 61.7% in one harness, 48.1% in another, and 38.4% bare [9]. Because harness choice changes benchmark results, evaluations should test the model and harness together.

7. Open-weight models caught up to frontier models. The top open-weight models now benchmark at a level comparable to that of top frontier models at a lower cost [3][4][5]. This was not true eighteen months ago. Open-weight models achieving frontier-level benchmark performance change the cost, control, and deployment trade-offs described in the other six points.

Across these observations, companies are trying to: 1) optimize costs without sacrificing productivity gains, 2) preserve operational freedom, and 3) ensure AI implementations can quickly incorporate innovations. To do so, they need an architecture in which models and harnesses can change without weakening governance.

Open-weight models improve cost efficiency, control, and flexibility over frontier models:

  • Commoditized Intelligence: As model intelligence becomes a commodity, open-weight options now provide intelligence parity with top frontier models at a fraction of the cost, enabling better ROI on AI deployments.
  • Data Sovereignty: Hosting models on controllable infrastructure gives teams authority over compliance, security, and data retention policies and reduces the risk of non-compliant changes in the future.
  • Complete Operational Autonomy: Open-weight models let teams run workloads that frontier guardrails may inhibit (e.g., cybersecurity response)

Source: [5] DeepSWE Leaderboard by Cost. Some of the top open-weight models compared against their proprietary equivalents, filtered at the authors’ discretion.

Unity Gateway serves open-weight and frontier models through a unified API with centralized governance controls, enabling teams to switch between models via configuration or smart routing [10][11] rather than through code changes or other abstractions [12][13].

The multi-model capability of Unity Gateway is becoming integral to customers’ AI strategies. Since January, the average number of unique models used per customer has increased from 4.2 to 7.1, an indicator of the options available on Unity Catalog and of the pursuit of higher-ROI models. Of those models, roughly ~40% were open-weight.

Source: Databricks’ internal data from the week ending January 5, 2026, through the week ending July 27, 2026. Created using Genie One.

Serving large open-weight models with competitive response times requires optimization to maintain cost efficiency at scale. Databricks addresses latency constraints by leveraging tailored inference engines and optimized kernels deployed on frontier GPUs. Independent evaluations from Artificial Analysis highlight these performance characteristics: for instance, GLM 5.3 (max) achieves an end-to-end response time (including input processing, reasoning, and generation) of 9.1 seconds on Databricks [15], performing favorably alongside top-tier managed endpoints [16].

Source: [15] GLM 5.3 Model Providers: Artificial Analysis

Here are some key features to help govern these models and control costs on Unity Gateway:

  • Smart routing sends sessions to the cost-efficient model for the task, so routine tasks shift off of frontier models [10][11].
  • Fallback chains automatically reroute in response to model rate limits or provider outages [14].
  • Budgets with spend caps by user, team, or use case prevent runaway spending [19][30]. These limits can be configured with varying levels of severity, from soft warnings to strict policies that reroute sessions to cheaper models.
  • Centralized governance for tools and skills. Along with built-in MCP servers, Unity Catalog supports registering External MCP servers that run through managed proxies and are audited centrally. Hence, agents get their tools with the same governance as their models [20]. Skills [21] can also be registered and governed, improving determinism and token efficiency for repeatable workflows.
  • Unified governance across open-weight, external, and frontier models. Connect external model providers (e.g., Amazon Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry) through model provider services [17] and route requests through the same central governance layer used for Databricks-hosted open-weight and frontier models [18]. Manage access, spend controls, and audit trails across your entire model portfolio from a single platform.

GLM 5.2 coincided with a sharp increase in open-weight usage on Unity Gateway. After GLM 5.2 became available in mid-July, its usage rose. At the same time, growth among Unity Gateway customers remained relatively consistent, suggesting that existing customers shifted more AI traffic toward open-weight models. Just one month after first being offered, GLM 5.2 already accounts for ~40% of open-weight tokens used on Unity Gateway, with most of that growth incremental. Both GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3's benchmark performance give customers another open-weight option to evaluate alongside GLM 5.2 [5].

To support this demand, Databricks announced a $3 billion fundraising round in July, and CEO Ali Ghodsi told CNBC the raise is partially about securing GPU capacity to host open models. "We are running out of GPUs everywhere... Japan, Korea, U.S., and India, so we just needed to get a lot of these, and that requires a lot of funding. So that’s what triggered this fundraiser for us" [22].

The harness your developers already live in can still run open-weight models hosted on Databricks. As of late July, models served on Unity Gateway, including GLM 5.3, can run inside provider coding harnesses such as Codex and OpenCode [12][26], with support for additional harnesses rolling out. The gateway exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints per harness, so the setup is just a config change. Point the harness at your workspace's gateway URL, or use the ucode helper with one line:

ucode codex --model system.ai.glm-5-3

Enterprises should plan for a portfolio of models because no single model or provider will lead in quality, cost, and policy fit for every workload. Of those to choose from, open-weight models now offer competitive intelligence at lower cost and greater control over data handling and governance policies. In contrast, frontier models remain useful where they deliver better results. Unity Gateway manages these options through common access controls, routing policies, budgets, and auditing. Omnigent extends that flexibility to the harness, so teams can change models or agent environments without rebuilding workflows.

The usage data in this article shows that customers are already moving in this direction. They are serving more models, directing more traffic to open weights, and using portable harnesses to broaden their options. The durable advantage is the ability to make those changes quickly as model options, quality, pricing, and policy requirements evolve.

[1] Nanda, M., Challapally, A., Pease, C., Raskar, R., & Chari, P. (2025, July). The GenAI divide: State of AI in business 2025 (Preliminary Findings from AI Implementation Research). Project NANDA, Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

entries.title: Claude Platform now supports native OpenTelemetry observability in Databricks MLflow
entries.summary: An agent can return a plausible answer while missing an important finding or reading the same source repeatedly...
entries.content:
Unify Claude observability into Databricks with native OpenTelemetry ingestion. Use collected traces with MLflow to find recurring failures and improve the agents.

  • OpenTelemetry for Claude Platform is now in Public Beta. The native OTel export brings Anthropic SDKs, Messages API and Claude Managed Agents into Databricks MLflow, with traces stored in Unity Catalog.
  • Use trace analysis and MLflow Issues to investigate bad answers and find repeated tool calls across runs and sessions.
  • Review answers with domain experts, then run evaluation with the same test cases to measure whether changes improve quality and reduce unnecessary work.

An agent can return a plausible answer while missing an important finding or reading the same source repeatedly. The answer alone won't explain why. Traces show the model and tool calls behind it, so you can investigate the failure, find related cases, and test whether a change helps.

Databricks MLflow is now a supported destination for native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform.. With native export to Databricks MLflow, developers using the Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API and Managed Agents can send native traces to Databricks and use MLflow to debug their agents and evaluate changes.

MLflow Tracing is built on OpenTelemetry, an open standard for collecting and exporting service signals. A trace records an agent’s execution as individual steps, called spans, such as model requests and tool calls. Claude’s native instrumentation generates these spans and exports them using the OpenTelemetry Protocol.

Databricks receives the spans through Zerobus Ingest and stores them in Unity Catalog tables linked to an MLflow experiment. You can inspect Claude traces alongside traces from other instrumented services, with the same tools for debugging and evaluation. Unity Catalog controls access to the data, which you can also query with SQL. With the combination of Zerobus and Unity Catalog, enterprises can get two crucial benefits: low-latency trace ingestion at high QPS plus the ability to govern access to the sensitive data stored in agentic traces.

In Databricks, open the Experiments tab and click Create Experiment. Under Trace storage location, keep Unity Catalog selected. Choose an existing catalog and schema. This creates new MLflow experiments linked to the Unity Catalog table that stores OpenTelemetry traces.

The detailed setup guide covers permissions and SQL warehouse requirements.

Set the Databricks destination using your workspace ID, region, and spans table. The Zerobus connection guide explains how to obtain a table-scoped OAuth token.

The new native OTel integrations cover Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API, and Managed Agents. For the Anthropic SDK, install the packages below and configure an OTel tracer provider and exporter to create spans for Anthropic SDK calls. Follow Claude Platform OpenTelemetry guide to send traces from the Messages API and Claude Managed Agent your Databricks destination.

Claude Code and Claude Agent SDK also support OpenTelemetry. To send their traces to the same destination, set these additional variables before starting your application:

Run your Claude agent, then open Traces in the experiment. Open a trace to inspect its model calls, tool activity, timing, and captured inputs and outputs. Note that inputs and outputs are captured only if you opt in by setting content mode to “full”.

Once Claude traces arrive in MLflow, you can use them throughout development. A trace provides a record for debugging, a case for expert review, and evidence for evaluating the next version of an agent.

An unexpected answer can come from missing context, a failed tool call, or how the model used a tool result. MLflow’s Analyze trace action brings Genie Code into the investigation. It examines the recorded execution and helps explain where things went wrong.

Ask follow-up questions about missing context, failed tool calls, or expensive steps, to inspect the relevant context behind the explanation. This helps you decide whether to revise instructions, improve a tool, or change the context available to the agent.

MLflow Issues, available in Beta, uses Genie Code to identify recurring quality and operational problems. It examines responses, tool calls, timing, errors, and assessments, then groups related findings with links to the supporting traces. Examples include repeated searches that waste tokens, missing arguments that cause tool failures, and responses that don’t follow the required format.

You can schedule detection to keep this analysis running as new traces arrive. Teams can choose how often it runs, use metadata or tags to focus on particular traffic, and customize the types of problems it looks for. After a fix, an issue monitor can track whether the problem returns. MLflow creates a scorer for the issue, evaluates recent traces to establish a baseline, and scores a sample of new traces to measure its frequency over time.

Some quality judgments require domain knowledge. MLflow Review Queues bring that expertise into the development process through selected traces and questions tailored to the agent.

Reviewers can assess the recorded request and response, explain what is missing, and provide an expected answer. Their feedback helps developers refine the agent and establish reference answers for subsequent evaluations.

A change to instructions, tools, or skills can fix one failure while introducing another. Traces also make agent behavior measurable. Run MLflow Agent Evaluation on Claude traces to test whether a change to prompts, skills, tools, improve the agent or regress.

For example, the following code executes an LLM judge to examine whether an agent makes redundant tool calls.

When the original and revised agents have run against the same cases, their evaluation runs can be compared using the same judges. Click Compare in MLflow UI to see scores and responses side by side, with the underlying traces available to explain remaining failures.

The same approach works for checks such as whether an agent followed a required workflow or used the appropriate tools. Testing and Refining Claude Code Skills with MLflow demonstrates how these checks and their rationales can guide improvements to skills.

The following resources cover connecting Claude to Databricks MLflow and using its traces during development:

  • Claude OpenTelemetry tracing guide: Native OpenTelemetry export configuration for Anthropic SDKs, Messages API, and Claude Managed Agents.
  • Tracing in Databricks with Unity Catalog: If you’re new to tracing in Databricks, this guide covers experiment setup, trace storage, and access.
  • Detect and monitor issues across MLflow traces: Recurring failure patterns, supporting trace evidence, and ongoing monitoring.
  • Evaluating Claude Code skills with MLflow: Behavioral judges and a repeatable process for testing and refining skills.

The first CTA item still needs the dedicated Claude integration-guide URL before publication.

entries.title: Declare and optimize with UNIQUE constraints on Databricks
entries.summary: Data teams often maintain uniqueness guarantees in their pipelines, but without a...
entries.content:
Represent multiple unique keys, reference them from foreign keys and use RELY to optimize joins and DISTINCT queries

by Yan Yan, Yuchuan Huang, Xinyi Yu and Gengliang Wang

  • Databricks UNIQUE constraints let teams declare multiple nullable or composite uniqueness guarantees beyond a table’s single PRIMARY KEY, and reference them with foreign keys.
  • Validate and continuously maintain these informational constraints before using RELY, which enables the optimizer to eliminate redundant joins and DISTINCT aggregations.
  • In 10 TB TPC-DS benchmarks, UNIQUE with RELY removed over 99.99% of shuffle and delivered up to 12× faster queries.

Data teams often maintain uniqueness guarantees in their pipelines, but without a flexible way to represent all of them in the table schema, users and tools cannot discover them and the query optimizer cannot safely leverage them. Business entities often have more than one value, or combination of values, known to be unique: a 

users
table might use 
user_id
as its primary row identifier while its data model also records separate uniqueness guarantees for 
username
, an email address, and 
(workspace_id, external_user_id)
.

Databricks already supports PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY constraints: a primary key identifies a table's rows, and foreign keys can reference it to describe relationships. A table can have only one primary key, however, and its columns must be non-nullable. 

UNIQUE
constraints, now available in Public Preview for Unity Catalog Delta tables in Databricks SQL and Databricks Runtime 18.2 and above, add a way to record the other uniqueness guarantees. A table can declare multiple 
UNIQUE
constraints, their columns can be nullable, and foreign keys can reference them. After you validate these constraints and mark them with 
RELY
, the query optimizer can also use them to eliminate unnecessary joins and aggregations. 

PRIMARY KEY
and 
UNIQUE
both record uniqueness, but they serve different schema roles:
Capability 
PRIMARY KEY
 
UNIQUE
Schema role Primary row identifier Additional uniqueness guarantee
Constraints per table One Multiple
Nullable columns No Yes

The following table has a primary key and two 

UNIQUE
constraints:

The two unique constraints illustrate different kinds of uniqueness. 

users_external_uq
applies to a column combination: each 
(workspace_id, external_user_id)
pair must be unique even though either value may appear in other pairs. 
users_optional_id_uq
applies to a nullable column. The following rows show which values satisfy that guarantee: 
user_id
 
optional_identifier
 Satisfies 
UNIQUE (optional_identifier)
?
1 
email:alice@example.com
 Yes
2 
NULL
 Yes
3 
NULL
 Yes
4 
email:bob@example.com
 Yes
5 
email:alice@example.com
 No - duplicates row 1

Like primary and foreign key constraints on Databricks, 

UNIQUE
constraints are informational and are not enforced when data is written. Declaring 
UNIQUE (optional_identifier)
, for example, does not cause a write containing duplicate non-null values to fail.

This separation lets the schema record a uniqueness guarantee maintained by an ingestion pipeline, an upstream system, or another data-quality process. The guarantee also becomes table metadata that users, tools, and applications can inspect.

A foreign key can reference a 

UNIQUE
constraint in addition to a primary key. For example, the composite 
UNIQUE
constraint declared above can be referenced as follows:

The referenced parent columns identify which unique constraint the foreign key targets. Child and parent columns correspond by position: 

workspace_id
maps to 
workspace_id
, and 
source_user_id
maps to 
external_user_id
. Their names do not need to match, but their types and positions must correspond. The 
REFERENCES
(parent) columns must be listed in the same order as the columns in the 
UNIQUE
constraint's definition; otherwise the constraint is still valid but join elimination silently won't fire.

To reference a single-column 

UNIQUE
constraint, explicitly name its parent column, for example, 
REFERENCES users (username)
. If the parent column list is omitted, 
REFERENCES users
targets the table’s primary key instead.

By default, a unique constraint is created with 

NORELY
. It records the intended schema semantics, but Databricks does not use it for correctness-dependent query rewrites. The following statement creates a constraint with this default:

After you have verified the data and ensured that your pipelines will continue to maintain the guarantee, you can drop and re-create the constraint with 

RELY
:

In this example, 

CASCADE
also drops any foreign keys that reference 
users_username_uq
, and they must be re-created after the unique constraint is added back. Without 
CASCADE
, 
DROP CONSTRAINT
uses the default 
RESTRICT
behavior and is rejected when dependent foreign keys exist.

A foreign key that references the unique constraint can also be declared with 

RELY
: 

RELY
is set independently on each constraint. It does not validate existing data or enforce the constraint on future writes. It allows Databricks to assume that the constraint is valid when optimizing queries. If the data violates a relied-upon constraint, a rewrite based on that constraint can produce incorrect results. You should therefore use 
RELY
only for guarantees that are validated and continuously maintained.

With 

RELY
, unique constraints can provide the information needed for eligible join and aggregation rewrites. Eligibility also depends on other guarantees required by the query, including nullability, as the examples below illustrate. This optimization support is available on Photon-enabled compute. The primary and foreign key blog describes constraint-based join and aggregation optimizations that 
UNIQUE
constraints can also enable. Since that post was published, 
RELY
support has become available for foreign keys and now for 
UNIQUE
constraints.

Some dashboards built on the same data need attributes from 

users
, so teams often create a shared view that always joins 
user_events
with 
users
. A dashboard that needs only information from 
user_events
may still inherit that join from the view. Its generated SQL can therefore look like the query below, even though it does not select any columns from 
users
:

Although the query returns no columns from 

users
, the optimizer cannot normally remove the join. An inner join could remove an event if no matching user exists, or duplicate it if multiple users have the same username.

The relied-upon constraints rule out both possibilities. The 

UNIQUE
constraint guarantees at most one matching user, while the foreign key guarantees that a match exists. Because 
user_events.username
is also 
NOT NULL
, every event has exactly one match. The join therefore cannot change the result, and the optimizer can read 
event_id
directly from 
user_events
.

The earlier primary and foreign key blog demonstrates the related 

LEFT OUTER JOIN
case, which needs only the at-most-one guarantee. This 
INNER JOIN
example also needs the foreign key to establish that a match exists.

With 

NORELY
constraints, the optimized plan retains the join:

When both constraints use 

RELY
, the optimizer can know that every event has exactly one matching user and remove the join:

In this example, 

user_events.username
is 
NOT NULL
, but the optimization also applies when it is nullable: Databricks will remove the join and add an 
IS NOT NULL
filter on the 
user_events.username
to preserve the inner join's handling of nulls.

We benchmarked this optimization on the TPC-DS SF10000 dataset, which represents a 10 TB scale factor. On the 28.8-billion-row 

store_sales
table joined to the 65-million-row 
customer
table, we declared 
customer.c_customer_sk
as 
UNIQUE
and defined a foreign key from 
store_sales.ss_customer_sk
. With 
RELY
on both constraints, Databricks eliminated the join, removed more than 99.99% of shuffle, and reduced median engine execution time from 23.6 seconds to 3.0 seconds - a 7.9x speedup.

BI tools and query builders often add 

DISTINCT
defensively because joins may produce duplicate rows. When the selected values are already unique, 
DISTINCT
removes nothing, but it can still require an aggregation and shuffle unless the optimizer can prove that the operation is unnecessary. A relied-upon 
UNIQUE
constraint can provide that proof.

Consider a 

user_identifiers
table with these two constraints: 
  • UNIQUE (user_id) RELY
    , where 
    user_id
    is 
    NOT NULL
  • UNIQUE (optional_identifier) RELY
    , where 
    optional_identifier
    is nullable

The table contains the following data, which satisfies both constraints:

For 

user_id
, the optimizer can use the uniqueness and non-null guarantees together:

The optimized plan contains no aggregation:

The aggregation is gone because the relied-upon constraint establishes that every 

user_id
is already distinct.

The equivalent query over 

optional_identifier
shows why the optimizer also considers nullability:

The optimized plan retains the aggregation:

Both constraints use 

RELY
, but the nullable constraint permits the two 
NULL
rows shown above. SQL 
DISTINCT
must collapse those rows into one, so the aggregation is still necessary.

Nullable 

UNIQUE
constraints can still enable the optimization when the query supplies the missing non-null guarantee:

The optimizer can remove the aggregation:

The filter removes the values that may repeat under nullable 

UNIQUE
semantics. The remaining values are guaranteed to be distinct, so Databricks can again avoid the aggregation.

We benchmarked this optimization on the same TPC-DS SF10000 dataset, which represents a 10 TB scale factor. On the 28.8-billion-row 

store_sales
table, we declared 
(ss_item_sk, ss_ticket_number)
as a composite 
UNIQUE
constraint and ran a 
DISTINCT
query over those columns. With 
RELY
, Databricks eliminated the 
DISTINCT
aggregation, removed more than 99.99% of shuffle, and reduced median engine execution time from 33.7 seconds to 2.8 seconds - a 12.0x speedup.

Before using 

RELY
, check that the data satisfies the guarantee. For a nullable 
UNIQUE
constraint, exclude rows containing 
NULL
because 
UNIQUE
permits those rows to repeat. This query finds duplicate non-null identifiers:

For a composite 

UNIQUE
constraint, group by every constrained column and add an 
IS NOT NULL
condition for each nullable column. You can also find child rows with no matching parent by using a left anti join:

These checks validate the current data. Your ingestion or data-quality pipeline must continue to maintain the guarantees after you enable 

RELY
.

After declaring or re-creating a constraint, you can confirm its definition in several ways:

  • SHOW CREATE TABLE
  • DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED
  • Unity Catalog INFORMATION_SCHEMA relations:
    • TABLE_CONSTRAINTS
    • KEY_COLUMN_USAGE
    • CONSTRAINT_TABLE_USAGE
    • CONSTRAINT_COLUMN_USAGE
    • REFERENTIAL_CONSTRAINTS

See Constraints on Databricks and the CONSTRAINT clause for complete create, alter, inspect, and drop syntax.

You can adopt 

UNIQUE
incrementally:
  • Declare existing uniqueness guarantees with the default 
    NORELY
    .
  • Reference unique keys from foreign keys where the relationship is part of the schema.
  • Validate and continuously maintain uniqueness and referential integrity in your data pipelines.
  • Use 
    RELY
    on the 
    UNIQUE
    constraint only after verifying uniqueness, and on the foreign key only after verifying that every applicable child value has a matching parent row.
  • Compare plans with 
    EXPLAIN
    to confirm eligible rewrites.

UNIQUE
constraints let a table record multiple uniqueness guarantees in addition to its single, non-nullable 
PRIMARY KEY
, and the constrained columns can be nullable. Foreign keys can reference a 
UNIQUE
constraint as well as a primary key. 
UNIQUE
constraints are informational by default; after validation, 
RELY
lets Databricks use them to optimize eligible joins and 
DISTINCT
queries.

entries.title: Lakebase Postgres is now generally available on Google Cloud
entries.summary: We're excited to announce that Lakebase Postgres is generally available on Google Cloud...
entries.content:
Power agentic and mission-critical workloads on Google Cloud with fully-managed, serverless Postgres.

  • Lakebase Postgres, a fully managed, serverless Postgres database, is now generally available on Google Cloud.
  • Autoscaling, scale to zero, instant branching, and point-in-time recovery help teams build and ship faster without managing database infrastructure.
  • Operational and analytical data share the same storage foundation so analytics, apps and agents run on a unified platform with no fragile pipelines to maintain.

We're excited to announce that Lakebase Postgres is generally available on Google Cloud. Teams building on Google Cloud can now run production-grade, serverless Postgres directly on the Databricks Data + AI Platform.

The Lakebase architecture separates compute from storage, which removes the resource conflicts and infrastructure overhead of traditional databases. It also shares the same storage layer as your analytical data which eliminates the need to build and maintain pipelines. The result is a Postgres database that scales with your application, shares one governance model with the rest of your data estate, and reduces your total cost of ownership.

For years, transactional databases and analytics platforms have been kept separate. Moving operational data into the lakehouse meant building and maintaining ETL pipelines, duplicating storage and accepting data lag. Now that AI agents act on data in real-time, that operational overhead becomes a bigger liability.

Instead with Lakebase, operational workloads run on the same platform, with the same security and governance as your analytics and AI. There is no siloed database to manage, no separate access controls to maintain and no data movement to keep in sync. Lakebase is a key component of the Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing (LTAP) architecture which allows organizations to unify their data foundation, decrease operational overhead and lower infrastructure costs.

Lakebase Postgres on Google Cloud delivers the capabilities for teams to ship faster:

  • Serverless autoscaling and scale to zero: Compute adjusts to match traffic and shuts off when idle, so you aren't paying for capacity you don't use.
  • Instant branching: Create isolated, zero-copy branches of production data in seconds to test changes safely.
  • Point-in-time recovery (PITR): Restore your database to a specific moment to recover from bugs or accidental deletions.

entries.title: Lakebase branching for CI/CD: lessons from 100 PR databases
entries.summary: The problem: testing against production data shouldn't take over 30 minutesSnorkel...
entries.content:
Copy-on-write branching makes isolated copies of production data fast and cheap for CI/CD testing and agentic use cases.

by Yasamin Tari and Kartik Mathur

  • Snorkel AI's CI/CD pipeline gives every open pull request its own Lakebase Postgres branch, a full read/write copy of production data that's ready in under a minute instead of over 30 minutes or longer, due to which they were never able to enable copy per PR.
  • Lakebase branches are copy-on-write, so 100 concurrent PR databases on a ~2.5 TB production dataset only add storage for the data each branch changes. Branch expiration (TTL) cleans up each branch automatically when its PR is done, so storage stays close to the size of production plus the changes from active PRs.
  • Private connectivity and Okta SSO support provide a governed and secure environment

Snorkel AI builds data development tools for AI teams, used by expert data annotators and frontier model providers. In this specific use case, Snorkel ships code through a CI pipeline built on Kubernetes. Every open pull request, plus ad-hoc commits, gets its own ephemeral Kubernetes namespace (a "PR namespace"). Developers deploy their branch there and run the full test suite before merging.

These tests are most useful when they run against real data. Snorkel's production database is an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Giving each PR namespace its own copy of that database was the hard part. Restoring a copy took about 20 minutes per environment, which is too slow when developers open PRs all day and the merge queue needs a fresh environment for each run. The alternatives (shared staging databases, trimmed fixtures, or synthetic data) bring back the problems production-like testing is supposed to solve: tests interfering with each other, stale schemas, and bugs that only show up with real data shapes.

Snorkel would consider Lakebase a success for CI/CD if it met these criteria:

  • Fast provisioning: A new PR branch is ready in under 60 seconds (p95).
  • Scale: About 100 concurrent PR branches at peak, each with independent reads and writes.
  • Compatibility: The existing application and CI suite run against Lakebase over standard Postgres, with performance comparable to Aurora and support for large JSONB/LOB columns.
  • Fresh data: The main branch stays within about 2 minutes of production Aurora through continuous DMS replication.
  • Security: Production data stays on private networking and never crosses the public internet, developers sign in with Okta SSO, CI pipelines authenticate as service principals.

Lakebase is Databricks' serverless Postgres database. Its storage and compute are separate, and it supports branching: you can create a new, isolated, writable branch of a database from any point in time, the same way you create a Git branch.

Branches are copy-on-write. Creating a branch is a metadata operation, so no data is copied when the branch is created. A new branch shares storage pages with its parent, and only the pages that the branch changes are written as new storage. For CI, this means:

  • Creating a branch takes seconds, not minutes. It doesn't depend on the size of the database.
  • Storage grows with the changes each branch makes, not the database size. Each of Snorkel's PR branches writes about 5 to 10 GB of changes on top of a ~1 TB base.
  • Compute is per branch and scales to zero. Each branch has its own autoscaling compute, which scales down to zero between CI runs. Even with 100 provisioned branches, Snorkel expects only about 20 to 30 to serve traffic at the same time, at around 5 queries per second each at peak.

1. Keep a fresh copy of production on the main branch. Lakebase is standard Postgres, so it works as a target for AWS DMS with no custom tooling. Snorkel points a DMS task at its production Aurora database and replicates it into the Lakebase project's main branch: a full load first, then ongoing change data capture that keeps main within about 2 minutes of production. Full LOB mode carries over the 10 to 20 MB JSONB values. The team already runs DMS, so there was no new replication pipeline to build or maintain. The main branch is the "golden copy" every PR branch starts from.

2. Create a branch when a PR opens. When a developer opens a PR, the CI pipeline calls the Lakebase API to create a branch from main, sets an expiration time on it, and passes the branch's connection details to the PR namespace. The branch is ready in under a minute.

3. Run tests against real data. The application in the PR namespace connects to its branch over standard Postgres. Tests can run migrations, write data, and change schemas without affecting production, main, or any other PR.

4. Delete the branch when the PR closes or test passes, with TTL as a backstop. When the PR is merged or closed, the pipeline deletes the branch. If that cleanup step doesn't run, the branch expires on its own when its TTL runs out.

Two security requirements ruled out other options, so they deserve their own section.

Private connectivity. Production data moves from Aurora to Lakebase, and from Lakebase to the CI cluster, over private networking instead of the public internet.

Identity. Snorkel has two kinds of database users: developers who connect interactively to debug a PR environment, and CI pipelines that run with no human involved. Okta SSO is built around interactive browser login, so we split the design by user type:

  • Developers: Okta is federated to the Databricks account, and users are provisioned through SCIM. Developers sign in with their usual Okta identity.
  • CI pipelines: Each PR namespace runs as a Databricks service principal (scoped per team or per repo), also provisioned through SCIM. The PR pod uses the service principal's credentials to get short-lived Lakebase OAuth tokens through the Databricks SDK, and refreshes them during long test runs. There are no long-lived database passwords in CI.
  • Auditing: Postgres audit logs record the service principal identity for each query, so every query can be traced to the pipeline that ran it.

Two Lakebase features make this pattern work at scale: copy-on-write branching and branch expiration (TTL).

Copy-on-write makes branches instant. A new branch doesn't copy any data. It points to its parent's existing storage pages, and only the pages the branch modifies are written as new storage. Creating a branch from a ~1 TB production copy takes about as long as creating one from a 1 GB database: seconds, not the ~20 minutes a full restore took. Each PR namespace gets its own isolated, writable copy of production right away.

Copy-on-write makes branches cheap. Every branch shares most of its data with main, so storage grows with the changes each branch makes, not with the size of the database. For Snorkel, that's about 5 to 10 GB per PR branch on top of the shared base. Compute is per branch and scales to zero when idle, so only the branches that are actively running tests use compute.

Branch expiration keeps it cheap over time. Copy-on-write saves the most when branches are short-lived. A branch keeps the version of data that existed when it was created. As DMS keeps updating main with production changes, a branch that stays around keeps holding those older pages, so the storage it uses grows over time. Setting a TTL on every CI branch means each branch is removed automatically once its PR is done. This keeps storage close to the size of the production base plus the changes from active PRs.

PR namespaces aren't the only workloads that need a disposable copy of production. AI agents that write SQL, run migrations, or change data also need a safe place to try things, and copy-on-write branching gives them one.

One branch per agent task. Each agent run gets its own branch of main. The agent can read real data, write to it, and even change the schema without touching production or any other agent's work. Creating a branch takes seconds no matter how large the database is, so it's practical to create one for every task.

Many agents in parallel. Storage only grows with the pages each branch changes, and each branch's compute scales to zero when it's idle. Running dozens of agents side by side costs about as much as the changes they make, not dozens of copies of the database.

Review the changes, or throw them away. Teams can check what an agent changed on its branch before applying anything to production. If the result isn't right, they delete the branch, and there's nothing to roll back.

TTLs clean up after agents. Agents can create a lot of short-lived branches. An expiration on each branch removes the abandoned ones automatically, the same way TTLs clean up CI branches.

Scoped identity for agents. Like CI pipelines, agents can run as service principals with short-lived OAuth tokens, so every query an agent runs can be traced in the audit logs.

  • Provisioning time: over 30 minutes before, under 60 seconds with Lakebase [VERIFY p95 measured]
  • Scale: Designed for about 100 concurrent PR branches on a ~2.5 TBproduction dataset
  • Compatibility: CI suite runs against Lakebase with "no major compatibility issues" / perf compared to Aurora
  • Adoption: Rollout to 60 to 70 developers across teams
  • Developer quote: "Previously we had to physically copy data and those copying jobs took hours and frequently ran into network and other bottlenecks with various CI platforms (github actions, circle ci etc). We were looking for a solution that passes our security and compliance requirements if data leaves our VPC"
  • One branch per PR, created from a continuously synced main branch.
  • Always set a TTL. Treat expiration as required, not optional. Match it to how long a PR or test run usually lasts.
  • Create a new branch instead of keeping an old one. If a PR needs fresher data, create a new branch from main. It takes seconds.
  • Let compute scale to zero. Most provisioned branches are idle at any given moment.
  • Use service principals and short-lived OAuth tokens for pipelines, and SSO for people.
  • Monitor storage per branch to catch long-lived branches early.

Ready to give every pull request its own production-like database? Get started with Lakebase and read the branching documentation to set up branch expiration in your CI pipeline.

entries.content:
With the new SAP Application Data Foundation, SAP and Databricks customers gain simpler, more performant access in SAP Databricks to data from SAP applications, across cloud and on-premises.

by Sanjay Chheda, Katie Cummiskey, Patrick Werns, Akram Chetibi and Qi Su

  • Databricks and SAP are expanding their partnership to provide expanded access to SAP application data across cloud and on-premises to accelerate time to value for advanced analytics and AI.
  • New Databricks capabilities including Genie, Lakeflow, Unity Gateway, and Lakebase come to SAP Databricks fully integrated with SAP Business Data Cloud.
  • Customers can put all their SAP data to work with the full range of the Databricks Data + AI Platform and AI capabilities.

Today's AI models are more capable than ever. What they still lack is the business context to understand how your company actually runs. For most enterprises, that context lives in SAP systems. Over 90% of Fortune 500 companies use SAP solutions to manage key business processes, enhance operational efficiency, and gain a competitive edge through data-driven decision-making.

Last year, SAP and Databricks introduced SAP Databricks, which natively embedded the Databricks Data + AI Platform in SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC). Since general availability, customers including Adidas, Zalando, and CAF have used SAP Databricks and SAP BDC Connect for Databricks to analyze, govern, and build AI on live, semantically rich SAP Data Products through zero-copy, bi-directional OpenSharing.

This week at SAP TechEd, we are announcing the next phase of our partnership. Now, we’re bringing together the expanded scope of Databricks to SAP Databricks in SAP Business Data Cloud. This makes it much easier and more performant to work with SAP enterprise data, allowing customers to realize AI value from their data.

Customers want to put their data to work: forecasting demand from years of order history, detecting anomalies in the financial close, optimizing procurement decisions, and grounding AI agents in how the business actually runs. Accessing SAP application data has been possible, but it has typically meant building and maintaining custom extraction pipelines that copy data, lose business context along the way, and fragment governance.

As SAP announced at TechEd, SAP Application Data Foundation makes data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. It provides a cloud-native way to access SAP application data, helping to lower total cost of ownership and reduce time to value. For SAP Databricks customers, that means:

  • No more custom extraction pipelines: SAP data products can be shared with SAP BDC Connect for zero-copy access, avoiding additional pipelines, data copies and silos.
  • AI built on SAP business semantics: Data engineers can build models on a semantically rich foundation, so analytics and AI reflect how the business actually runs.
  • The full Databricks Data + AI Platform on SAP data: Genie, Lakeflow, Unity Gateway and Lakebase turn that data into enriched data products, apps and agents.

For example, a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, while planning its move to the cloud, can use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring years of order history into SAP Databricks. Its data engineers can enrich that history with third-party data and build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines, and keep that work as they move to the cloud.

The expanded partnership plans to bring the full range of Databricks data and enterprise AI capabilities to SAP Databricks, embedded within SAP BDC.

  • Genie: An AI coworker that gives every team instant access to governed data and AI, with enterprise context built in. Genie delivers the context in core SAP data to every team and agent. A planned bi-directional integration between Genie and Joule can bring those answers and actions into SAP experiences.
  • Lakeflow: A unified data engineering solution to ingest, transform, and orchestrate data, so teams can build pipelines that combine SAP data with IoT, CRM, and third-party sources.
  • Unity Gateway: Multi-AI governance and cost control across agents, tools, models, and MCPs, so teams can scale AI on SAP data with guardrails and spend controls in place.
  • Lakebase: The first serverless, mission-critical Postgres database built for AI apps and agents that helps teams build operational data apps on SAP and enterprise data.
  • One place to govern data and AI. Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway govern data, models, and agents across SAP and non-SAP data.
  • Choice of architecture. Customers can use SAP data inside SAP BDC with SAP Databricks or bring governed SAP data or data products they create based on SAP data into an existing Databricks estate, with any model on any cloud.
  • Faster time to value. SAP and Databricks are expanding our go-to-market partnership, with joint teams in the field so joint customers can accelerate their AI transformation based on critical enterprise data helping customers get value faster.
“Data is the foundation for enterprise AI. By bringing the latest scope of Databricks into SAP Business Data Cloud, we’re combining SAP’s deep understanding of business processes and mission-critical applications and agents with Databricks’ industry-leading data platform. With that, we help customers turn their enterprise data into a powerful foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise.” - Philipp Herzig, Chief Technology Officer, SAP SE
"This partnership brings together the most critical business data in the enterprise, SAP data, with the leading Data + AI Platform, Databricks. With the new SAP Application Data Foundation and SAP Databricks in BDC, companies can finally bring all of their SAP data together and unleash the full capabilities of the Databricks platform to drive business insights. They can also combine Genie with Joule to deliver that business context to every team and agent so they can get trusted answers and act on them."- Michael Kiermaier, SVP Business Strategy and Operations, Databricks

SAF-Holland, a global manufacturer of chassis components for trailers, trucks, and buses, uses SAP BDC and SAP Databricks to unify more than 100 million records of customer, delivery, and material data. The company applies machine learning to predict the reliability of customer delivery schedules. SAF-Holland now generates analyses 5x faster than with traditional reporting approaches, and turns complex SAP data into planning and supply chain insights in minutes instead of weeks.

"Opening the SAP data ecosystem to Databricks has unlocked better analysis for our internal teams and ultimately helps us deliver better outcomes for our customers."- David Gund, Senior Manager of Global Digital Intelligence, SAF-Holland

SAP Databricks and SAP Business Data Cloud Connect for Databricks are available today. Talk to your SAP or Databricks account team to learn about the new SAP Application Data Foundation and expanded SAP Databricks capabilities and plan your path to analytics and AI on all your SAP data.

entries.title: Wealth Management Client Onboarding Needs More Than AI
entries.summary: Wealth Management client onboarding can stall even when every system has done its job. The document is collected...
entries.content:
How governed case context connects evidence, supervised agents, and human judgment to move clients from first document to funded account.

  • Task-level AI speeds up document processing and KYC screening, but wealth management client onboarding still stalls when evidence, case state, and decisions remain fragmented across systems.
  • Governed case context gives AI agents and human reviewers a shared, versioned view of each case, including its evidence, exceptions and decision history.
  • On Databricks Data + AI Platform, supervised AI agents coordinate the full journey with governance, traceability, and human oversight. Measure the impact through cycle time, manual touches, and approval-to-funding time.

Wealth Management client onboarding can stall even when every system has done its job. The document is collected, the screening result is back, and the workflow task is complete. Yet the case is still waiting because someone has to determine what changed, which evidence is current, and who owns the exception.

For the client, those boundaries are invisible. They experience one journey and expect their information and progress to move with them. Inside the firm, however, that journey crosses customer relationship management (CRM), document, know your customer (KYC), screening, custody, and workflow systems, each holding a different part of the case.

Firms have invested in making those individual steps faster, and AI is accelerating them further. But a quicker extraction, screening summary, or routing decision does little if the next team must still reconstruct the case, reconcile the evidence, and reopen work that appeared complete.

Onboarding still loses time at these handoffs. A modern platform has to connect the case across systems, coordinate work as conditions change, and preserve the controls and human judgment that the process depends on. When it doesn't, the cost accumulates between systems.

The first cost is what clients feel most directly: time.

In Singapore, opening a private banking account takes about 6 weeks, with complex cases taking longer. In May 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said initiatives from an account-opening workgroup co-led by MAS and industry were expected to bring that median within one month.

Inside the firm, it shows up in staff time. The Capgemini World Wealth Report 2026 found that 60% of 144 wealth executives lacked a unified client view. The same report found that 1,317 relationship managers across 16 markets said operational work consumed 41% of their time. That figure covers wealth operations broadly, not onboarding alone, but it shows how much capacity routine coordination can absorb.

The onboarding journey itself spans many teams. A 2024 EY report of more than a dozen global asset managers found that more than half involved at least 10 teams in onboarding. Yet only 15% reported strong integration with their CRM systems.

“More than half of global asset managers involve at least 10 teams in onboarding, yet only 15% report strong CRM integration.”

A 2024 KPMG and Private Wealth Management Association study of 35 Hong Kong private wealth institutions cited onboarding demands as a factor in rising costs and deteriorating client experience.

The findings span markets, populations, and supervisory regimes, and each needs to be read in context. Across them, the pattern is consistent - fragmented client information, with many teams stitching the journey together.

Firms absorb that coordination through staff hours, repeated evidence searches, manual reconciliation, exception handling, and control-history preparation. Integration, maintenance, and change testing add more cost while account opening and funding wait.

Faster tasks do not always produce a faster onboarding journey. A system can finish its work on time and still leave the case stalled at the next handoff.

AI can accelerate each task further, but it does not automatically remove friction between systems.

AI is already moving into wealth and asset management. In a 2025 EY survey of 100 decision-makers, split evenly between wealth and asset management firms, 95% of firms reported scaling generative AI across multiple use cases, while 78% were exploring agentic AI. Yet translating this momentum into measurable business value remains a challenge, with only 27% of executives reporting substantial business impact from GenAI.

Looking at the work itself explains the gap. AI can extract document fields, summarize a screening result, or recommend the next workflow action. Each capability may improve a task within a single application, yet the handoff still depends on current evidence and a clear record of what changed. Teams also need to know whether earlier work must be revisited.

AI agents make that dependency more important because routing work across specialist agents and approved tools requires a shared case state. That state must show what is complete, what has gone stale, and which exception blocks the next step. Without it, faster orchestration can reproduce the same fragmentation it was meant to reduce.

Governed case context is a current, versioned, source-linked view of each client onboarding case. It brings together the evidence, case state, completed controls, open exceptions, agent activity, and decision history. Because the context is versioned, teams can see what changed, what the change affected and whether earlier work needs to be revisited.

Different parts of onboarding can live in different places. Core client and custody records may remain in their assigned systems, while evidence processing, controls, models, and case workflows can run on the Databricks Data + AI Platform. Governed case context connects that work in one governed view, as the diagram below illustrates, while preserving record ownership and decision authority. On Databricks, Unity Catalog centralizes access controls, lineage and auditability for this context, while open table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg support reliable data management and interoperability across systems.

Governed case context is useful only when it helps the next agent or reviewer understand and advance the case. A practical test is whether they can answer four questions without reconstructing its history:

  • What evidence is current, and which source and version support it?
  • What work is complete, what has changed and which results may now be stale?
  • What remains unresolved, and what is the next permitted action?
  • Which work can an agent or approved tool perform, and where must an authorized reviewer decide?

With those answers in one place, a governed supervisor agent can resume work from the current case state. It can assign independent tasks to specialist agents, call approved tools, and bring in a reviewer when judgment is required. It can also flag conflicting evidence and assemble a complete package for review, while the evidence, changes, and actions behind that package remain attached to the case.

The value comes from putting this context to work across the journey. A modern platform must keep it current, coordinate agents and people around it, and preserve visibility and governance from the first piece of evidence through the final decision.

Putting governed case context to work requires four platform capabilities. Together, they address the friction identified earlier: rebuilding the case at each handoff, coordinating work manually, governing access to sensitive data, and measuring tasks without seeing the whole journey.

  • Maintain a current view of the case:

    As evidence arrives, controls run and decisions are made, the platform should update the governed context and preserve its links to the underlying sources. Systems assigned to particular records can remain authoritative, while agents and teams work from the same versioned context. On Databricks, Lakeflow Connect brings changes from supported source systems into the platform, Databricks AI Functions extract and classify new evidence and Lakebase maintains the live transactional state used by onboarding applications.

  • Coordinate agent work while people retain authority:

    A governed supervisor agent should select the next permitted action based on the current case state, sending defined tasks to specialist agents or approved tools and bringing in a qualified reviewer when judgment is required. People retain responsibility for exceptions, overrides and onboarding approval. On Databricks, Supervisor Agents can coordinate specialist agents and approved tools, including Unity Catalog functions, MCP services and Genie Agents (formerly Spaces), over governed enterprise data.

  • Govern data, tools and actions:

    Onboarding involves personally identifiable information (PII) and other sensitive records. Each agent should have access only to the data and tools required for its task, with sensitive fields masked or withheld where appropriate. Agent activity should remain traceable and reviewable. On Databricks, Unity Catalog provides fine-grained access controls, masking, lineage and auditability across governed data and AI assets, while Unity Gateway extends that governance to agent runtime by controlling which models and MCP tools each agent can call, applying guardrails, routing requests across models, enforcing budgets and rate limits, and logging every request.

  • Measure end to end:

    Teams should monitor agent quality, latency, reliability and escalation alongside cycle time, manual touches, rework, exceptions and approval-to-funding time. The operating picture should also include integration changes, duplicated data movement and the effort required to prepare control evidence. Databricks Apps can embed Databricks AI/BI dashboards within the queue and case workspace, giving operations and compliance leaders a consolidated view of journey performance alongside active cases.

Together, these capabilities turn governed case context into an operating model. The architecture below shows how the context, supervised agents, and human review work together in practice.

The architecture puts the four capabilities into a recurring operating loop around each case. Information can arrive from source systems, while evidence processing, controls, risk models, and onboarding workflows run on the platform. Each result returns to governed case context with its source references and history attached, giving the next agent or reviewer the current state of the case.

A governed supervisor agent reads that context and selects the next permitted action. Depending on the case, it can call an approved tool, assign work to a specialist agent, or involve a reviewer. When new evidence makes an earlier result stale, it can reopen the affected work instead of restarting the entire case. It also monitors completion and freshness, flagging missing or conflicting control results before the case moves forward.

A simple example shows how the loop works. Consider a case waiting on a required document. The supervisor can identify the gap, prepare a client outreach email for review and pause any work that depends on the missing evidence. Once a reviewer approves the outreach and the document arrives through the designated channel, the case context updates. The supervisor can then trigger document processing, rerun only the affected checks and route the case to its next permitted step.

In this illustrative design, each specialist agent has a defined job:

  • A document intelligence agent reads submitted files, extracts the required information, and flags missing evidence.
  • A KYC and screening agent brings together results from identity, KYC, and screening controls.
  • A risk analysis agent evaluates verified case facts against defined rules and control results.
  • A case summary agent prepares a draft assessment for review.

Each result returns to governed case context with its supporting evidence and source references. The supervisor uses that updated state to determine whether another agent should act, human review is required, or the case can move forward.

People retain decision authority. From a controlled workspace, reviewers can inspect evidence, request additional information, resolve an exception, record an override with its rationale or make a decision within their authority. Their actions become part of the case history and may trigger another agent task or a targeted rerun. Case Recommendation remains a draft assessment. Alert disposition, risk acceptance, and onboarding approval remain with the systems and reviewers assigned that authority.

Governance follows the work through the entire loop. Fine-grained access limits each agent to the data and tools required for its job. Agent traces record what each agent did, how long it took and its estimated model cost. Teams can use that history to evaluate quality, spot regressions and investigate failures. These traces support AI and model-risk oversight, while authorized decisions remain in the business record. Together, traces and decision records give compliance and audit teams a reconstructable account of each case: what evidence was reviewed, which controls ran, what each agent produced, and who approved, overrode or escalated the outcome, and why. That record supports AML/KYC record-keeping and exam readiness, because firms can show how each decision was reached instead of piecing the history together after the fact.

The reviewer workspace records human actions, while the application maintains the live case state required by the workflow. After an authorized decision, a controlled integration records the approved outcome in the system assigned to own it. On Databricks, the reviewer workspace can run as a Databricks App, with Lakebase maintaining the live case state.

The value of this operating model must be measured across the entire journey, from the first evidence collected through account funding. Otherwise, a faster agent or control may simply move the delay to the next handoff.

The architecture creates value when it improves the whole onboarding journey. Faster agent responses matter, but the real test is whether cases move sooner, teams spend less time coordinating work, and controls remain effective.

Start with one high-friction path. Choose an onboarding journey where handoffs, rework and delays are already visible. Before the pilot begins, align wealth operations, compliance, data, and technology leaders. Agree on the required evidence, who owns each record and decision, where human judgment is mandatory, and which actions the supervisor may trigger.

Establish the baseline before changing the workflow. Measure the current journey across three areas:

  • Cost and capacity: Cost per completed onboarding and the advisor, operations, and compliance hours spent on each case.
  • Journey performance: Median and 90th-percentile cycle time, approval-to-funding time, manual touches, systems accessed, document rework, exceptions, incomplete cases, and abandonment.
  • Technology and control: The cost of running and changing integrations, duplicated data movement and the effort required to assemble control, lineage and audit evidence.

Together, these measures surface work that often disappears inside team queues and system handoffs. They also show whether governed case context has reduced repeated reconciliation and evidence searches or simply moved the work elsewhere.

Set the success thresholds before the pilot begins. Evaluate speed, staff effort, agent quality, trace completeness and control effectiveness. The supervisor and specialist agents should reduce avoidable handoffs and prepare a more complete case for review. Their traces should make the work easier to evaluate and investigate.

Exception, override and reopened-case rates still require root-cause and quality review. An increase could indicate a control problem. It could also mean the new process is detecting issues that were previously missed.

Read the results across the journey:

  • If median cycle time improves while the 90th percentile does not, complex cases are still getting stuck.
  • If agent processing speeds up while approval-to-funding time remains unchanged, the bottleneck has shifted.
  • If manual touches fall while control-evidence preparation stays flat, the final review package still needs work.

Scale when the gains hold from first evidence collected through account funding and control effectiveness remains intact. The standard for modern onboarding is straightforward: move the case faster, make every agent action reviewable and preserve human authority wherever judgment matters.

Faster document processing, screening, or routing does not resolve fragmented evidence, case state, and decision history. Onboarding can still stall at the next handoff when teams must determine what changed, which work remains valid, and who should act.

Governed case context is a current, source-linked and versioned view of an onboarding case. It connects evidence, case state, control results, exceptions, agent activity and decision history so agents and reviewers can work from the same context.

A governed supervisor agent can route work across specialist agents for document intelligence, KYC screening, and risk analysis, and approved tools while involving reviewers when judgment is required. Fine-grained access and traces make agent activity reviewable, while people retain authority over exceptions, overrides and onboarding approval.

No. Core records may remain in CRM, custody, or other assigned systems, while evidence processing, controls, models, and workflows run on the Databricks Data + AI platform, with Unity Catalog governing data, models, and agent tools. Governed case context connects the work while preserving record ownership and decision authority.

Firms should measure results across the entire onboarding journey rather than relying on agent speed alone. Useful measures include cycle time, approval-to-funding time, manual touches, rework, staff effort, integration cost and control effectiveness. Firms should scale when improvements hold end to end and agent actions remain reviewable.

Start with one high-friction onboarding journey and measure the impact from first evidence through account funding. See how Databricks helps financial services firms build governed, traceable agentic workflows with people in control.

entries.title: Deliberate decisions and enterprise AI value
entries.summary: AI progress is moving quickly. Expectations are rising, experimentation is spreading...
entries.content:
Discover how senior data and AI leaders are balancing momentum, accountability and flexibility to turn AI ambition into sustained enterprise value.

by Jack Yallop and Lexy Kassan

  • Why AI progress needs grounded decisions when readiness, evidence and expectations are uneven.
  • What senior leaders are learning about investment, ownership, human judgment and strategic flexibility.
  • How 5 leadership disciplines help turn AI ambition into sustained enterprise value.

AI progress is moving quickly. Expectations are rising, experimentation is spreading and organizations are under pressure to show meaningful returns. But the decisions that matter most are rarely about whether AI is possible. They are about where to commit, what to prioritize and how to move forward when the evidence is still incomplete.

That is the focus of Deliberate Decisions: How Grounded Leadership Is Advancing the Path to Enterprise AI Value, a report produced by DataIQ in partnership with Databricks. The report brings together perspectives from senior data and AI leaders who are making these choices in real organizations.

The report draws on open peer discussions at DataIQ Guild 2026, an invite-only think tank for senior data and AI leaders. Across industries, leaders described a similar challenge: they are expected to maintain momentum while technology, operating models, workforce impact and business cases continue to evolve.

Early AI success can raise expectations faster than an organization can absorb. Pilots and proofs of concept can multiply before teams have the capacity to assess, govern and support them. Ownership can become unclear as AI crosses functions, while roles and workflows change faster than organizations can define them.

The answer is not to slow down until everything is certain. Nor is it to commit to every promising use case. The report points toward a more grounded form of leadership: making deliberate, evidence-based choices while preserving the ability to adapt.

Report snapshot:

  • Two days of peer discussion at DataIQ Guild 2026 underpin the report.
  • Five recurring pressures are shaping the current data and AI environment.
  • Five leadership disciplines emerged to help leaders respond deliberately.
  • Four stages describe the AI adoption journey: concerned, curious, comfortable and competent.

Download the report now: Deliberate Decisions: How Grounded Leadership Is Advancing the Path to Enterprise AI Value

Five leadership disciplines emerged from the discussions at DataIQ Guild 2026:

  • Confidence grounded in reality: test AI progress against evidence, readiness and the realities of production.
  • Enterprise choices, not demand-led reactions: prioritize business outcomes over isolated enthusiasm or use-case volume.
  • Leadership through influence, not control: create clarity, ownership and proportionate governance across the enterprise.
  • Human judgment as a strategic capability: preserve the authority, context and skills people need to challenge AI outputs.
  • Stability without rigidity: anchor purpose, decision rights and standards while keeping roles and technology choices flexible.

To lead data and AI today is to navigate a constant tension between commitment and flexibility. Every investment, architecture and operating model decision requires leaders to balance confidence in what they know today with openness to what may change tomorrow.

The Databricks perspective in the report identifies four foundations for navigating that tension:

  • Context grounds AI in trusted, governed data.
  • Control gives leaders confidence that innovation can progress responsibly and securely.
  • Cost keeps sustainable adoption aligned with ambition and efficiency.
  • Choice preserves the ability to evolve as technologies, models and business priorities change.

These foundations are reflected in Databricks capabilities such as Lakebase, a governed transactional foundation for building and running data and AI applications and agents, and Genie, which helps people and AI agents access organizational context responsibly and efficiently.

Together, they reinforce the report’s central message: progress does not require waiting for certainty. It requires making informed decisions, knowing where to commit and preserving choice.

A successful pilot is not the same as an AI capability that is ready for production. The report explores the difference between early results and sustainable adoption, including the operational support, governance, skills, monitoring and cost model that become visible once AI enters a live workflow. As Thomas Gebetsroither, Data & Analytics Operations Lead, Axpo Trading & Sales, mentioned:

“The cost is not just the model or the tool. It is the security, the support, the adoption, the governance and the operating model around it. If those costs are invisible, the business case is incomplete.”

Leaders will find a practical way to test whether an AI initiative can remain useful, reliable and affordable beyond the conditions of a bounded experiment.

AI demand can come from the board, business functions, employees and vendors. But demand alone cannot determine the agenda. The report looks at how leaders start with a well-defined business problem, make trade-offs visible and prioritize work with enterprise-scale potential.

It also examines why AI investment may be better managed as a portfolio. Organizations can make a range of initial bets, increase investment as evidence strengthens and stop or redirect work that does not justify further commitment.

“Not every investment needs to pay back in the same way. Some will deliver direct value, some will generate learning and some will create capabilities that can be reused across the organisation.”- Gavin Goodland, Chief Data Officer, National Grid

AI adoption is not owned by one team. Business outcomes, workflow change, risk, adoption and ongoing costs are distributed across the organization. You will learn why clear decision rights are not enough unless a business owner is also prepared to own the outcome and its consequences.

This matters because an approved use case without committed ownership can create a new problem rather than solve an existing one.

“We want the business to be accountable. Any of the use cases that we get prioritized need to have an impact on the long-range plan.”- Bharathi Rajan, VP – Data, Digital & AI, Swire Coca-Cola

As AI handles more execution, people spend more time framing problems, interpreting results and deciding what happens next. The report examines why human authority must be explicit, how organizations can build role-appropriate AI fluency and why automating away opportunities to develop expertise can create long-term risk.

The central question is not whether humans remain somewhere in the process. It is whether they still have the authority, context and time to challenge an output when it matters.

Organizations need enough continuity to know where accountability sits and which principles apply. At the same time, technology choices, roles and operating models need room to evolve. As the report delineates, the challenge for leaders is not to protect people from automation. It is to avoid automating away capabilities the organisation cannot replace.

The report offers a way to identify the fixed points that matter — purpose, decision rights, standards, human authority and business ownership — while keeping other decisions flexible and, where possible, reversible.

Deliberate Decisions does not predict which technology will win. It focuses on the judgment calls leaders are making now: what to commit to, where to push back, how to move forward responsibly and how to preserve choice as conditions change.

For leaders moving from experimentation toward enterprise AI value, the report provides a practical framework and shared language for making trade-offs visible. Rather than presenting a use case as an isolated technical project, connect it to the business outcome it should change, the evidence supporting the next investment and the ownership required to sustain it.

That creates more useful conversations with executive sponsors and business teams. It also makes it easier to assess readiness, stop, redirect, or redesign work when the evidence changes, treating course correction as disciplined leadership rather than failure.

Before approving the next use case, ask:

  • What evidence shows that this capability is ready for the conditions of the live enterprise?
  • Who owns the outcome, including adoption, operating consequences and ongoing cost?
  • Which parts of this decision should remain flexible if technology, roles or business priorities change?

These questions will not remove uncertainty. They can improve the quality of the decisions made in its presence.

The full report develops these ideas through five leadership disciplines and perspectives from the DataIQ Guild community. It is designed to help leaders compare their own decisions with the choices other organizations are making as AI becomes more consequential.

Download the full Deliberate Decisions report to explore the leadership model and the practical actions behind it.

Look beyond pilot results. AI is ready to scale when the organization can support, govern, adopt and afford it in a live workflow.

Start with a clearly defined business problem and enterprise value. Manage initiatives as a portfolio, increasing investment as evidence strengthens.

A business owner should be accountable for the outcome, adoption, operating consequences and ongoing costs, with clear decision rights across teams.

Define which decisions remain human-owned and give people the authority, context and time to challenge, override or stop an AI system.

Set fixed points for purpose, standards, ownership and human authority, while keeping roles, operating models and technology choices open to review.
