entries.title: Announcing General Availability of Real-Time Mode for Spark Declarative Pipelines on Databricks
entries.summary: We introduced Real-Time Mode (RTM) last year which enabled customers to build low-latency, operational use cases...
entries.content:
Bring sub-second latency to your most time-critical operational workloads with declarative flows and sinks

by Jerry Peng, Abhay Bothra, Sudhanva Huruli, Navneeth Nair, Anant Pingle and Murali Talluri

  • Announcing General Availability of Real-Time Mode (RTM) on Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP), delivering end-to-end processing latencies in the millisecond range for operational streaming workloads.
  • Real-Time Mode eliminates the need for separate specialized engines such as Apache Flink, unifying batch, ETL, and low-latency streaming under a single framework.
  • Real-Time Mode enables real-time computation and instant writes to operational stores via ForEach sinks, powering time-critical use cases like fraud detection and live personalization.

We introduced Real-Time Mode (RTM) last year which enabled customers to build low-latency, operational use cases. This was a game changer because it allowed customers to process streaming data in milliseconds, up to 100x faster than traditional micro-batch architecture. Furthermore, they no longer needed to maintain separate, specialized engines like Flink alongside Spark, eliminating duplicate codebases, fragmented governance models, and operational overhead.

Today, we are announcing RTM in Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP) is now Genearally Available. SDP has become the standard way to build streaming and ETL pipelines on Databricks, automatically handling dependency resolution, incremental processing, orchestration, failure recovery, and data quality enforcement. With RTM, customers can build operational, low-latency pipelines while retaining all of those SDP benefits. Whether for fraud scoring, real-time alerting, or pushing fresh features to operational stores, you can now use SDP across all of these use cases.

RTM is an evolution of the Spark Structured Streaming engine that achieves end-to-end latencies in the millisecond range. It does this by streaming data continuously, running all query stages simultaneously, and passing data between stages as soon as it is produced. For the full architecture deep dive, read the blog, “Breaking the microbatch barrier: The architecture of Apache Spark Real-Time Mode.”

RTM can support any workload that benefits from turning data into decisions in milliseconds. Some example use cases include fraud detection, live personalization, real-time recommendation systems, and real-time feature computation. We benchmarked RTM against Apache Flink on actual customer workloads performing feature computation, and RTM is up to 92% faster than specialized engines like Flink. Below are the benchmarks. For more information on the datasets and queries referenced, see this GitHub repository.

Customers are increasingly defaulting to SDP for their ETL workloads. With RTM, SDP now supports all streaming workloads, including operational low-latency streaming, enabling customers to use a single framework across all pipelines. One framework means one observability stack, one billing model, and no fragmentation across different APIs.

SDP serverless takes it further. There is no compute to choose and no cluster to size. You get sub-second latency, without any complex infra tuning, while paying only for the cores your query uses. RTM flows also get SDP features such as versionless upgrades and low-downtime maintenance, which reduce both the operational work and the disruption of upgrades.

One use case where RTM on SDP has immediate impact is real-time feature computation. ML models for fraud detection or personalization depend on fresh signals, such as a user's total transaction amount over the last 10 minutes, to make accurate predictions. Computing these rolling-window aggregations and landing them in an online store within milliseconds is where RTM on SDP closes the gap. The Databricks Feature Store uses this exact architecture to deliver end-to-end p99 latency of 200ms from Kafka to the online feature store.

Real-Time Mode requires the pipeline mode to be 

continuous
and 
spark.databricks.streaming.realTimeMode.enabled
set to 
true
takes over.

Real-time mode requires an update flow. Use 

dp.create_sink()
to define the output target, then use the 
@dp.update_flow
decorator with 
pipelines.trigger
set to 
"RealTime"
and 
target
pointing to the sink.

For supported sources and sinks, see the documentation.

Use cases like fraud detection or real-time personalization require not only that features be computed in real time but also that they land in a queryable, low-latency store. A fraud model needs a customer's latest transaction before it clears, and a personalization engine needs to read what a user just browsed.

Today, you can write to any custom sink like Lakebase, Redis, or any other OLTP store from SDP using a ForEach sink. Define the writer, register it as a 

foreach_sink
, and wire it to an 
update_flow
.

Features land in your operational store within milliseconds of being produced, with no offline-to-online sync in between. Applications and models can query them at ultra-low latency. 

What’s next for RTM on serverless?

  • Running RTM pipelines at lower cost: Bin-pack multiple RTM flows into a single pipeline instead of each query standing up its own resources. The system also auto-tunes source and shuffle partitions based on workload, so users skip manual sizing.
  • Expanded sink support: Native Lakebase sink for SDP, with built-in batching, automatic retries, and UC-managed authentication.

RTM extends Spark Declarative Pipelines into a new class of workloads, operational, latency-sensitive applications that demand immediate response to streaming data. By bringing sub-second latency to the SDP APIs your team already uses, it eliminates the need to operate a separate framework or engine for your most time-critical pipelines. Whether you're building fraud detection pipelines, personalization engines, or ML feature computation systems, real-time mode gives you the latency your application demands with the simplicity of SDP.

Real-Time Mode on Spark Declarative Pipelines is now Generally Available.

Check out the following resources to get started with RTM on SDP:

  • Documentation: Use Real-Time Mode on Lakeflow pipelines
  • Documentation: Connect to Lakebase streaming sink
  • Documentation: Use a ForEach sink to write each row in pipelines
  • Code examples: Real-Time Mode on SDP examples

What is Real-Time Mode (RTM) in Spark Declarative Pipelines?

Real-time mode (RTM) lets Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP) process streaming data with end-to-end latency in the millisecond range. It streams data continuously, runs all query stages at the same time and passes data between stages as soon as it's produced. Real-time pipelines benefit from SDP's orchestration and automatic failure recovery.

Is Real-Time Mode available in Spark Declarative Pipelines?

Yes. Real-time mode on Spark Declarative Pipelines is now generally available. It brings the real-time mode already available in Spark Structured Streaming to SDP pipelines.

How do I turn on real-time mode in a pipeline?

Set the pipeline to 

continuous
mode and set 
spark.databricks.streaming.realTimeMode.enabled
to 
true
. Then define an update flow with 
pipelines.trigger
set to 
"RealTime"
and a target that points to a sink.

Can a real-time pipeline write to Lakebase or another OLTP store?

Yes. Define a ForEach sink with a writer that implements 

open
, 
process
and 
close
, then point a real-time flow at it. This works for Lakebase, Redis or any other OLTP store.

What use cases is Real-Time Mode in Spark Declarative Pipelines built for?

Real-Time Mode is built for operational workloads that turn streaming data into decisions in milliseconds. Examples include fraud detection, live personalization, real-time recommendations and real-time feature computation. The Databricks feature store uses this architecture to reach a p99 latency of 200 ms from Apache Kafka to the online feature store.

entries.title: What to Look for in a Postgres Managed Service: A Technical Buyer's Checklist
entries.summary: Managed is a label, not a specification. Evaluate a cloud database managed service...
entries.content:
Traditional managed Postgres excels at transactional workloads but compromises on analytics queries—and most evaluation checklists miss this gap. If you're evaluating Postgres as a hybrid transactional-analytical engine, you need different criteria.

  • A managed Postgres service should be evaluated on what it can prove under failure, recovery, and production load, not just the features it advertises.
  • The key checks include high availability, disaster recovery, PostgreSQL compatibility, security, scaling, total cost, operational control, and portability.
  • A production workflow should test the provider's claims with failover, point-in-time recovery, load, and migration tests before the service is adopted.
  • Lakebase Postgres provides managed, serverless Postgres with automatic high availability, autoscaling, and Databricks security and governance capabilities.

Managed is a label, not a specification. Evaluate a cloud database managed service on what it proves under failure and recovery, not on what its feature page lists.

A Postgres managed service is a PostgreSQL database where the provider operates the underlying infrastructure and automates database administration, such as patching, backups, failover and scaling. How much the provider actually manages varies by service, which makes "managed" a label rather than a complete specification. Major cloud providers, including AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, offer managed PostgreSQL services, as do database-focused vendors.

A provider might advertise high availability, automated backups, or enterprise security, but those claims do not tell platform engineers or DBAs what happens when a primary fails, how quickly a database can be restored, or whether a required PostgreSQL extension is supported. When a problem does surface in production, what matters is how quickly the team can find and resolve it.

Platform engineers, DBAs, data architects, and engineering managers evaluating a Postgres managed service for production. It covers the areas that tend to cause problems after migration, such as operational control, high availability, disaster recovery, scaling, and so on. Each section looks at what the provider should support, the questions worth asking during an evaluation, and how to test the answers in a pilot. If you're a DBA or platform engineer planning a move, use this article as a working checklist rather than a one-time read.

A managed Postgres evaluation should cover more than database provisioning and day-to-day administration. The table below gives teams a starting point for the capabilities to verify and the answers that should trigger a closer review.

Area What to verify Red flag
Operational scope Who handles patching, upgrades and tuning, and what database controls remain available "Managed" only covers the virtual machine and operating system
High availability Automatic failover, committed-transaction guarantees, and whether failover works across availability zones No stated Recovery Point Objective (RPO) or manual promotion
Backups and disaster recovery Point-in-time recovery (PITR), restore options, retention, cross-region recovery, and recovery objectives Disaster recovery is available only through a support request with no stated RPO or Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
Scaling and performance Resize behavior, read replicas, connection pooling, storage, and input/output operations per second (IOPS) model Vertical scaling requires extended downtime
Security and compliance Private connectivity, identity and access controls, customer-managed keys, audit logs, and compliance scope Public connectivity is required or encryption keys can only be controlled by the provider
Compatibility and extensions Supported PostgreSQL versions, extensions, drivers, parameters, and superuser restrictions A critical extension or required PostgreSQL capability is unsupported
Migration Supported migration paths, logical replication, and change data capture (CDC) options Large databases can only migrate through dump and restore
Pricing and total cost Compute, storage, IOPS, backups, replicas, network egress, and extended-support costs Only the compute price is clear
Operations Database metrics, logs, alerts, and access to PostgreSQL-level support Limited database observability or no escalation to PostgreSQL experts
Portability and exit Standard exports and logical replication to another PostgreSQL environment Data can only leave through a proprietary format or support request

The first thing to verify is where the provider's responsibility ends and the database team's responsibility begins. A managed service should take care of infrastructure and routine database operations without removing the PostgreSQL controls a production workload depends on. Providers referring to a service as fully managed don't always mean the same thing.

Start with maintenance. Ask whether minor version updates are automatic, whether teams can choose a maintenance window, how much notice providers give before changes, and whether updates require a restart or failover. Major version upgrades deserve separate attention. PostgreSQL supports each major version for five years, so teams should understand how long the provider supports each version and what happens when that support ends. Ask for the end-of-life date the provider uses for each version. Generally, the less notice a provider gives before updating a database, the harder it is to plan around.

Configuration access is another common source of surprises. Managed services often restrict superuser access and limit parameters or commands that could affect the underlying infrastructure. Before migrating, check which roles are available, which parameters can be changed, whether 

ALTER SYSTEM
is supported, and which PostgreSQL commands are restricted. For example, some services let you edit a set of parameters through a console or API but block the ALTER SYSTEM command entirely.
  • Ask how minor and major version upgrades work, including maintenance windows, notifications, and end-of-support policies.
  • Ask which PostgreSQL roles, parameters, and commands are restricted.
  • Prove it by applying a minor update in the pilot and measuring the effect on active connections and application traffic.
  • A red flag is a service that calls itself fully managed while leaving patching, upgrades, or critical maintenance tasks to the database team, or one that cannot clearly document its configuration and upgrade limits.

Automatic failover in Postgres databases means that the service can automatically promote a standby in another availability zone and clearly state what happens to committed transactions during failover. High availability protects against failures within a region, but it is not the same as disaster recovery.

Ask whether the standby uses synchronous or asynchronous replication, what recovery point the provider supports, and whether the database endpoint stays the same after promotion. Applications will usually need to reconnect after existing connections drop, so the provider should document the expected behavior. In a multi-node cluster, confirm which nodes can be promoted and how applications find the new primary. Ensure your connection pools and drivers, whether in Java, Python, or another language, handle reconnects cleanly.

  • Ask whether high availability uses synchronous replication and whether the standby runs in a separate availability zone.
  • Ask how long failover typically takes and whether committed transactions are preserved.
  • Prove it by triggering a failover, timing the recovery and checking application errors, committed writes and replication behavior.
  • A red flag is manual promotion or no clear guarantee around committed transactions.

Backups and disaster recovery (DR) are important in databases. Verify that backups can restore the database to a known point in time and that the provider clearly states its recovery objectives. RPO defines how much data a workload can afford to lose. RTO defines how long the database can remain unavailable.

Ask whether the service continuously archives the Write-Ahead Log (WAL), how long point-in-time recovery remains available, and whether restores are self-service. For disaster recovery, check whether cross-region replication is continuous or periodic, whether failover is automatic or manual, and whether the provider publishes RPO and RTO targets. Automated backups combined with continuous WAL archiving are what make point-in-time recovery and reliable data restoration possible.

  • Ask whether you can restore the database to a specific timestamp and how long the process typically takes.
  • Validate critical records and application reads after the restore.
  • Run a disaster recovery drill if the provider supports one and document the recovery steps.
  • A red flag is disaster recovery that is only available through a support request or has no published RPO or RTO.

Verify how the service handles growth in compute, storage, connections, and read traffic. Scaling should not introduce unexpected downtime or require you to manage infrastructure manually.

Ask whether compute can scale vertically, whether read replicas are available, how storage and input/output operations per second (IOPS) scale, and whether connection pooling is built in. For services with autoscaling, check what triggers scaling, how quickly capacity changes, and whether scaling affects active connections or transactions. On most managed services, scaling CPU and RAM is typically a few clicks or a single API call, which lets teams match capacity to user growth rather than launch new infrastructure.

  • Ask whether vertical scaling requires a restart or failover.
  • Ask how storage grows and whether there are limits on connections, IOPS, or replicas.
  • Prove it by running representative production load and testing a scale-up during active traffic.
  • Measure query latency, connection errors and application behavior before and after scaling.
  • A red flag is scaling that requires extended downtime or has undocumented capacity limits.

Validate how the service protects data in transit and at rest, controls database access, and connects to the network. Security features should match the organization’s existing identity and compliance requirements rather than require a separate operating model.

Ask whether private connectivity is supported, how Identity and Access Management (IAM) integrates with database roles, and whether Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) are available. Also check audit logging, encryption controls, and the provider’s compliance scope. Ask whether applications can connect through a private IP address, a public one, or both. Most managed providers enforce encryption at rest and in transit and apply routine OS patches and security updates automatically, so confirm which compliance frameworks, such as HIPAA or GDPR, the service supports.

  • Ask whether databases can run without public internet access.
  • Ask how database activity, administrative actions, and authentication events are logged.
  • Verify that encryption keys can be rotated or revoked without disrupting the database.
  • Prove it by connecting through the intended private network path and testing access with different roles.
  • A red flag is a service that requires public connectivity, provides limited audit visibility, or does not support the security controls required by the organization.

You should check that the service supports the PostgreSQL versions, extensions, drivers, and configuration options the workload depends on. Compatibility should be tested against the actual application rather than inferred from the provider’s claim that it supports PostgreSQL.

Verify which PostgreSQL versions are available, how quickly new major versions become supported, and which extensions are enabled. Check support for extensions such as pgvector, PostGIS, and any application-specific dependencies. Also confirm which parameters, roles, and PostgreSQL commands are restricted. Check whether superuser restrictions affect existing tables, functions, or extensions, and whether objects that exist in your current database would need to change. Self-managed teams often run PostgreSQL on Ubuntu or another Linux distribution with full OS access, so dependencies on the operating system should be identified early.

  • Ask for the complete list of supported extensions and version-specific limitations.
  • Ask whether application drivers, ORMs, and standard PostgreSQL tooling work without modification.
  • Test any required extensions and database parameters before migration.
  • Prove it by restoring a representative schema and running the application’s migrations and integration tests.
  • A red flag is a critical extension being unsupported or compatibility depending on undocumented workarounds.

For AI workloads, pgvector support is important for vector search alongside transactional workloads.

REPORT

The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise

Verify how the provider supports both initial data migration and the final cutover. A migration method that works for a small database may not be practical for a production system that must keep serving traffic during the move.

Ask whether the service supports logical replication, Change Data Capture (CDC), native PostgreSQL tools, and third-party migration services. For migrations from other database engines, check which source systems are supported and how schema conversion, data validation, and application changes are handled. Moving a production DB from other databases such as Oracle or SQL Server also requires schema conversion and application testing.

  • Ask whether large databases can migrate without extended downtime.
  • Ask how ongoing changes are replicated during the migration window.
  • Prove it by migrating a representative dataset, running validation checks, and measuring the final cutover time.
  • A red flag is a migration process that depends entirely on dump and restore or requires extended application downtime.

Your migration solution should account for dependencies across your data environment and minimize disruption.

A managed service can add costs for storage, backups, high availability, replicas, network transfer, and other usage-based resources. Much of the savings over self-managed deployments comes from avoiding on-premises hardware and maintenance, so find out which features are included in the base price and which are paid add-ons.

Check how compute, storage, IOPS, backups, replicas, and network egress are charged. Check whether pricing changes with autoscaling, standby capacity, or higher availability configurations.

  • Model both normal and peak usage, including storage growth and backup retention.
  • Calculate Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) over the expected contract period.
  • Prove it by building a 12-month TCO model covering compute, high-availability standby capacity, IOPS, backups, replicas and network egress for your expected workload. Do not use only the compute line.
  • A red flag is pricing that only shows database compute while leaving storage, backups, replicas or network costs unclear.

Usage-based pricing can make costs easier to align with workload demand, but teams should still model realistic traffic patterns before committing.

A production service needs enough visibility for database teams to understand what is happening when performance or reliability degrades. Infrastructure metrics alone are rarely enough to diagnose PostgreSQL issues.

Ask whether the service exposes database metrics, logs, and query-level information, and whether teams can configure alerts for important conditions. Find out what access support engineers have during incidents and whether PostgreSQL specialists are available for escalations. Look for dashboards with real-time visibility into system metrics, and check whether logs can be filtered by database or user and whether you can sort events by time or severity. Also consider whether your team has the skills to troubleshoot PostgreSQL issues using only the provider's tooling.

  • Ask which PostgreSQL metrics, logs, and query statistics are available.
  • Ask whether monitoring data can be exported to the organization’s existing observability platform.
  • Prove it by generating a controlled performance issue and using the available tools to identify the root cause.
  • A red flag is limited database-level visibility or a support model that cannot investigate PostgreSQL-specific problems.

For large deployments, ask whether the provider’s tooling can surface patterns across all your databases, not just per-instance metrics.

A managed Postgres service should make it possible to move data and applications to another PostgreSQL environment without depending on proprietary export processes.

Ask whether standard PostgreSQL tools and logical replication can be used to move data out. Find out whether any provider-specific extensions, APIs, or storage formats would make an exit harder. The more unique provider-specific features an application depends on, the harder an exit becomes.

  • Ask how a complete database export works and whether it can run without provider support.
  • Ask whether logical replication can stream data to another PostgreSQL environment.
  • Prove it by restoring an export into a separate PostgreSQL environment and running application tests.
  • A red flag is data that can only be exported through a support request or a proprietary format.

A pilot should test the provider’s claims against a workload that resembles production. A feature checklist can show what a service offers, but controlled failure and recovery tests show whether those capabilities work when they matter.

Start with a representative database, application traffic, and the PostgreSQL extensions the production system requires. Then test the areas most likely to affect the decision. If you prefer a phased approach, start with a non-critical workload and expand the pilot a bit at a time.

  • Run a failover and measure recovery time, connection recovery, and lost transactions.
  • Restore the database to a specific point in time and compare the result with the expected RPO and RTO.
  • Apply representative peak load and test scaling while the application remains active.
  • Run migration and rollback tests, including any required extensions and application changes.
  • Test monitoring and support escalation.

Record the results against the original requirements and treat failed tests as decision points.
